extra.message: SQL Injection in Login Endpoint — Attacker bypasses authentication entirely, extracts all user credentials from the database, modifies or destroys database contents, and chains with the dashboard XSS by injecting XSS payload as username that gets stored in the session cookie. [verified: User-controlled username/password from request.form.get are directly interpolated into a raw SQL f-string query (line 33) with zero parameterization, escaping, validation, or middleware — classic SQLi allowing auth bypass and data exfiltration.]

Plaintext Password Storage in Database — All user passwords are stored in plaintext. Any database compromise (via SQL injection or direct file access through the Docker volume mount) immediately exposes all credentials, enabling credential stuffing and account takeover. [verified: Passwords are stored as plaintext TEXT column (line 14) and inserted without hashing (line 15); login compares raw values with no bcrypt/scrypt/PBKDF2.]

Forgeable Plaintext Session Cookie — Attacker impersonates any user (including admin) by simply setting the session cookie to the target username. No cryptographic knowledge or token guessing required — the username is the entire session token. [verified: The session cookie set at line 38 is the raw plaintext username with no signing, HMAC, encryption, or server-side store — trivially forgeable by setting session=admin in the browser.]

Missing Authentication on Dashboard Endpoint — Any anonymous user can access the dashboard without credentials, bypassing the entire login mechanism. The dashboard is treated as sensitive but has no access control whatsoever. [verified: The /dashboard route (line 43-47) has no authentication decorator, middleware, or server-side session validation; it falls back to 'guest' with no credential check, exposing a post-login resource to unauthenticated users.]

Cross-Site Scripting in Dashboard via Session Cookie — Attacker achieves persistent XSS through a chained SQLi+XSS attack, executing arbitrary JavaScript when any victim (or the attacker themselves) visits /dashboard with a crafted session cookie. [verified: The 'session' cookie value (user-controlled, forgeable plaintext) is interpolated directly into HTML via f-string (line 47) with no escaping or sanitization — cookie-based stored XSS.]

Missing HTTP Security Headers — Application is vulnerable to clickjacking, MIME-type sniffing attacks, lacks XSS mitigation via CSP, and transmits over plain HTTP without HSTS enforcement, exposing users to downgrade and man-in-the-middle attacks. [verified: The Flask app (lines 4-57) sets zero HTTP security headers — no X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, CSP, HSTS, or Referrer-Policy on any response.]

Missing CSRF Protection on Login Endpoint — Attacker can perform login CSRF to force a victim to authenticate under an attacker-controlled account, enabling session hijacking or tracking of victim actions within the application. [verified: The state-changing /login POST (line 25-41) has no CSRF token, no SameSite cookie attribute, and no CSRF middleware — login CSRF is feasible.]

Missing Brute-Force Protection on Login — Attacker can perform unlimited credential guessing against the login endpoint, brute-forcing weak passwords through dictionary attacks without any throttling or lockout. [verified: No rate limiting, account lockout, or throttling exists on the /login endpoint (lines 25-41); unlimited brute-force attempts are possible.]

Session Cookie Missing Security Flags — Session cookie is accessible to JavaScript (enabling theft via XSS), transmitted over plain HTTP (enabling network sniffing), and sent on cross-site requests (facilitating CSRF attacks). [verified: The set_cookie call at line 38 specifies no HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags — cookie is accessible to JS, sent over plain HTTP, and included on cross-site requests.]
